questions.stem: Which catalyst does the industrial hydration of ethene use?

options.text: Concentrated phosphoric acid
options.explanation: Phosphoric acid is the named catalyst for adding steam across the double bond.

options.text: Concentrated sulfuric acid
options.explanation: Sulfuric acid appears in other organic reactions; the hydration catalyst is phosphoric.

options.text: Iron filings
options.explanation: Iron catalyses other industrial processes and plays no part here.

options.text: Enzymes from yeast
options.explanation: Enzymes belong to the fermentation route, not to the ethene route.

questions.stem: Which temperature and pressure does the hydration of ethene need?

options.text: About 300 degrees Celsius and 60 to 70 atmospheres
options.explanation: Both figures are stated conditions of the industrial process.

options.text: About 30 degrees Celsius and normal pressure
options.explanation: Those are roughly the fermentation conditions applied to the wrong route.

options.text: About 300 degrees Celsius at normal pressure
options.explanation: The high temperature is right but the pressure must also be raised to 60 to 70 atmospheres.

options.text: Room temperature with a pressure of 60 to 70 atmospheres
options.explanation: The pressure is right but the reaction also needs the raised temperature.

questions.stem: Where does the ethene for this process come from?

options.text: The cracking of hydrocarbons
options.explanation: Cracking hands over ethene as a valuable by-product in bulk.

options.text: The fermentation of glucose
options.explanation: Fermentation makes ethanol directly and never supplies ethene.

options.text: Burning ethanol in air
options.explanation: Burning destroys ethanol into carbon dioxide and water.

options.text: Distilling sea water
options.explanation: Water supplies steam for the reaction but no carbon skeleton at all.

questions.stem: When the reaction is complete, how is unreacted ethene removed from the chamber contents?

options.text: It boils off first because its boiling point is far lower than those of ethanol and water
options.explanation: At minus 103 degrees the gas leaves long before either liquid vaporises.

options.text: It is filtered out through paper
options.explanation: Filtration separates solids from liquids, not gases from liquids.

options.text: It is neutralised with sodium carbonate solution
options.explanation: Neutralisation removes acids, and ethene is not an acid.

options.text: It is frozen solid at the bottom of the chamber
options.explanation: Ethene is the coldest-boiling component and leaves as gas, not as a solid.

questions.stem: Which method finally separates the ethanol and water?

options.text: Fractional distillation
options.explanation: The two liquids boil at 78 and 100 degrees, so distillation divides them.

options.text: Filtration
options.explanation: Both substances are dissolved liquids, so nothing can be caught on a filter.

options.text: Adding calcium chloride solution
options.explanation: Calcium chloride removes ethanol as an impurity in a different practical, not here.

options.text: Decanting
options.explanation: Ethanol and water mix completely, so no layer forms to pour off.

questions.stem: Why must air be kept out of a fermentation vessel?

options.text: The yeast must respire without oxygen for ethanol to be the product
options.explanation: Anaerobic respiration of glucose is what delivers ethanol; oxygen would redirect the chemistry.

options.text: Oxygen would poison the yeast instantly
options.explanation: Yeast survives oxygen fine; the issue is which products respiration then makes.

options.text: Air would dilute the glucose solution
options.explanation: Gases bubbling through do not dilute a solution appreciably.

options.text: Oxygen would evaporate the ethanol as it formed
options.explanation: Evaporation depends on temperature, not on the presence of air.

questions.stem: Why is about 30 degrees Celsius the optimum fermentation temperature?

options.text: Below it the reaction is too slow and above it the enzymes stop working
options.explanation: Rates fall when cold, and excess heat changes the enzyme shapes that do the catalysing.

options.text: Yeast only survives at exactly 30 degrees
options.explanation: The yeast tolerates the 25 to 35 degree band; 30 is simply the best compromise.

options.text: Ethanol boils at 30 degrees so higher temperatures lose the product
options.explanation: Ethanol boils at 78 degrees, well above the fermentation range.

options.text: Sugar dissolves fastest at exactly 30 degrees
options.explanation: Dissolving is not the bottleneck; enzyme activity is.

options.text: C6H12O6 gives 2CO2 plus 2C2H5OH
options.explanation: One glucose molecule yields two carbon dioxides and two ethanols.

options.text: C2H5OH + O2 gives CH3COOH + H2O
options.explanation: That is the oxidation of ethanol, the chemistry of a different note entirely.

options.text: C6H12O6 + 6O2 gives 6CO2 + 6H2O
options.explanation: That is aerobic respiration, which releases energy and makes no ethanol.

options.text: CO2 + H2O gives C6H12O6 + O2
options.explanation: That is photosynthesis, the reverse direction of carbon fixation.

questions.stem: Why is fermentation described as a batch process?

options.text: Alcohol near 15 percent kills the yeast, so the vessel must be emptied and restarted
options.explanation: Each batch ends when the yeast is killed by its own product, and a fresh charge begins.

options.text: The ethanol is collected one drop at a time
options.explanation: Collection method is irrelevant; the stopping-and-restarting is what makes it a batch.

options.text: The reaction only runs during daylight hours
options.explanation: Light plays no part in fermentation chemistry.

options.text: Each batch requires a different kind of sugar
options.explanation: The sugar source can stay the same; the yeast dying off forces the restart.

questions.stem: How is the ethanol and water mixture from fermentation separated?

options.text: Fractional distillation
options.explanation: The boiling-point gap between ethanol and water is exploited in the usual way.

options.text: Filtration through paper
options.explanation: Nothing solid remains once the yeast has done its work.

options.text: Adding sodium carbonate until fizzing stops
options.explanation: That step removes acidic impurities in the ester practical, not ethanol from water.

options.text: Letting the water evaporate into the air
options.explanation: Ethanol evaporates faster than water, so waiting loses the product first.
